people.mina: Mina Harker, a young dark-haired Englishwoman of about twenty-five, hair pinned up, a plain dark dress with a white high collar; no mark on her face
people.seward: Dr John Seward, a doctor of about thirty, dark hair, bare clean-shaven face with no beard and no moustache, dark frock coat
people.jonathan: Jonathan Harker, a grown man of twenty-six with prematurely white hair and a young face, clean-shaven, dark suit
people.arthur: Arthur Holmwood, Lord Godalming, a tall young English nobleman of about thirty in black mourning clothes
people.quincey: Quincey Morris, a tall lean Texan of about thirty with a moustache, in a travelling coat

beats.text: On a crowded Paddington railway platform in 1893, steam and iron girders behind, a sweet-faced young woman holds out her gloved hand to the doctor, who has just recognised her; porters and travellers around them.

Inside a gas-lit carriage of the London Underground railway in 1893: the doctor and the young woman sit opposite each other on wooden benches, her small typewriter case on the floor at her feet, the dark tunnel wall beyond the window.

A doctor's study at an asylum: the young woman stands in the doorway, surprised and curious, looking at a phonograph with a brass horn on the table, the doctor rising from his chair beside it, alone in the room.
In the study, the doctor recoils with a horror-struck face, one hand raised as if to ward off the question; the young woman watches him gravely, a terrible feeling coming over her.
In the study, the young woman cannot help smiling, and the doctor grimaces sheepishly, caught out like a boy, one hand on the phonograph.
In the study, the doctor turns deathly pale and shakes his head, while the young woman, seated by the phonograph, quietly offers to copy his diary on her typewriter.
In the study, the young woman points to a great batch of typewritten pages on the table and speaks earnestly; the doctor looks at the papers, his resistance giving way.
The doctor carries the heavy phonograph up a staircase in the asylum himself, the young woman going ahead with a candle, lamplight on the banisters.
Late afternoon in the doctor's study: he sits absorbed in reading thick bundles of typewritten diaries, papers spread all over his desk, the light fading at the window, utterly forgetting the time.
At the door of her sitting-room, the young woman meets the doctor; her eyes are red and swollen with weeping, the phonograph visible on the table behind her; he looks at her with deep concern.
In a lamplit sitting-room, the young woman lays her hand on the doctor's hand and speaks very gravely to him; he looks down, moved.

In the study at night, the young woman lies back in her chair, powerless and pale after listening, the phonograph earpieces fallen in her lap; the doctor has jumped up with a horrified face and is reaching for a decanter of brandy.
Morning at the asylum: a young man with prematurely white hair, full of energy, strides in through the hall carrying a travelling bag and shakes the doctor's hand.

The station-master's office at Whitby in 1893: the white-haired young man leans over a desk studying the invoice for fifty great boxes of earth, the station-master pointing at a ledger, sea light through the window.
The goods office at King's Cross station in 1893: the white-haired young man questions a foreman in a cap, who shows him a delivery book; behind them, carts and stacked crates in the goods yard.
The busy counting-house of a London carrier's office in 1893: clerks at high desks look up an entry in a great day-book for the white-haired young gentleman; a telephone on the wall.
The old ruined chapel of Carfax at night: fifty great wooden boxes of earth stacked in the dust and shadows, cobwebs, a shaft of moonlight from a broken window. No people.
A drawing-room at the asylum: the young woman receives two visitors, a tall young nobleman in black mourning and a lean Texan with a moustache, a painful meeting; grey afternoon light.
In the drawing-room the tall young nobleman in mourning holds a thick typewritten manuscript and asks the young woman whether she wrote all of it; she nods.

The tall young nobleman in mourning has turned away and covered his face with his hands; the Texan lays a hand on his shoulder for a moment before quietly leaving the room; the young woman watches with pity.
In the drawing-room, the young woman and the tall young nobleman in mourning clasp hands, his eyes wet, hers kind.
In a long asylum corridor by a window, the lean Texan with a moustache stoops and takes the young woman's hand and kisses it, moved; evening light through the window.
beats.at: He saw that I was in earnest

beats.text: The young woman stands alone in the dim corridor, her eyes red, one hand at her throat, deeply moved, looking after the men.
